title: The Northern Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino del Norte
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The Camino del Norte is the coast road to Santiago. It starts at Irun, on the French border, and follows the Bay of Biscay west through the Basque Country, Cantabria and Asturias. In Galicia it turns inland, meets the Camino Francés at Arzúa, and walks the last stretch to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. The app's catalog gives it ~820 km. It is long, green and often wet, and its hills come one after another.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this long road is your Camino, how its thirty-seven walking days fall region by region, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, one chapter for each region, and the chapter on other roads, which covers the choices this Camino offers: the two ways into Galicia, the links to the Camino Primitivo, and the roads that branch from this one.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your day. Each one says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.

On this road they disagree more than most. No single body publishes the whole Camino del Norte: the Basque Government, Cantabria, Asturias and the Xunta de Galicia each publish their own part, in their own stages and their own style. Every distance here carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate, and the book names the source of each set of figures. Where something depends on the season (a boat, a closed path, a river after rain, a hostel that opens only in summer), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way. Each stamp is a
sello
. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules, which the chapter on arriving sets out. A
ría
is a long sea inlet where a river meets the ocean; this road crosses many.

The road crosses four regions with their own languages. Official pages give Basque and Spanish names in the Basque Country, Spanish and Asturian names in Asturias, and Galician names in Galicia. This book uses the Spanish forms in the Basque Country, Cantabria and Asturias, and the Galician forms of the Xunta de Galicia in Galicia, such as Lourenzá and Sobrado dos Monxes.
Carry what you need, walk gently, and take your time over the long hill.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Camino del Norte, also called the Camino de la Costa, begins at Irun, across the Bidasoa river from Hendaye in France. The walk starts at the international Santiago bridge. It crosses four regions: the Basque Country, Cantabria, Asturias and Galicia. Asturias describes it as the continuation of the road that runs through the west of France, the "Camino de Soulac".

In Galicia the road leaves the sea at Ribadeo and goes inland, by Mondoñedo, Vilalba and the monastery of Sobrado dos Monxes. At Arzúa it meets the Camino Francés, and the Xunta de Galicia adds that the Camino Primitivo, which joined the Francés at Melide, is also on that road. The three routes walk the last ~38 km together.
How long is it?
The app's catalog gives ~820 km. Other sources do not agree with it, or with each other:

items.t: Wikipedia says ~817 km from Irun, and the Confraternity of St James says ~825 km "depending on route chosen".
The Asturias tourism pages give ~815 km for the whole Camino de la Costa.
Spain's national tourism site says the road is ~800 km long, but its own figures for the four regions (~175 km, ~170 km, ~280 km and ~220 km) add up to ~845 km.
The Spanish Wikipedia counts ~828 km from Hendaye to Arzúa, and ~867 km to Santiago.
The Cantabria guide and the Spanish government's 2015 announcement of the UNESCO listing give ~936 km for the listed route.

spans.t: The pages do not always say what they count. Starting points differ (Hendaye, Irun or Hondarribia), and so do the variants. Plan on ~820 km, and know that the stage lists add up to more: the thirty-seven days of this book come to ~867 km, because they follow the official lists with all their loops.

Stage counts vary as much. The four regional lists have eight, nine, thirteen and eight stages: thirty-eight in all. The national tourism site recommends 8 or 9, 7 or 8, 9 to 11, and 8 to 10 for the regions, which is 32 to 38 days. This book follows thirty-seven walking days, named by their stage towns. With rest days, count five to six weeks.
Why the north?

The Basque Government says many researchers consider the coast road one of the oldest pilgrim routes to Compostela, with evidence of pilgrims in the first decades of the ninth and tenth centuries, on roads in use since long before. It was the safer way, it says, compared with Navarre, then threatened by Muslim armies. Asturias says the same of its own part: when the kings of the eleventh and twelfth centuries promoted the Camino Francés, the coast and the Primitivo stayed busy because they ran through lands that were already Christian. The Confraternity of St James adds that much of the route follows the line of an old Roman road, the Via Agrippa.

It was also a road for those who came by sea. The Xunta says pilgrims came by land or by sea from England, Flanders, Germany and Scandinavia, and that the route came into prominence in the late Middle Ages, when sea pilgrimages were at their height. Asturias writes that in the thirteenth century the road thrived on pilgrims who started at Irun and on those who landed at the ports of Bermeo and Bilbao. Cantabria's government, when it defined its stretch of the Way in 2015, wrote that the Way has been in use for more than twelve hundred years, and it records pilgrims' hospitals in many of the towns the road crosses.
In 2015 UNESCO added the northern routes, among them this one, to the Camino Francés, which had been listed in 1993.
Who walks it now

Wikipedia, reporting the Pilgrim's Office statistics, gives the Norte a share of about 4 per cent of pilgrims in 2024, a small part of the whole. The Confraternity of St James calls it a good alternative for a longer and slightly quieter first Camino, and Wikipedia says it is less travelled because of its changes of height.
What it feels like

The Confraternity describes the shape of it. The first week in the Basque Country takes you from the coast into a hinterland of hills and woods. After Bilbao the road returns to the sea, with beaches, seaside towns and the roads that join them. Between Avilés and Ribadeo you are often by the sea, with few hills. At Ribadeo you turn inland and the country becomes more undulating, and the highest point of the route, ~710 m, comes shortly after Miraz. It is easy to miss, because the slope is gentle and nothing marks it.

Asturias calls the road a kind of opposite of the Camino Francés. Where the Francés crosses mountains and then the dry plateau, the Norte passes the frontier and runs beside the Cantabrian Sea. Because the road follows the coast, it crosses many rivers, and the Confraternity says there is more walking on tarmac than on the Francés. The next chapter says what that means for you.
How hard is it?

The app's catalog rates the Camino del Norte 4 on a scale of 1 to 5. It rates the Camino Francés 3, the Camino Primitivo 4 and the Camino Inglés 2. The Norte earns its 4 differently from the Primitivo, which is short and steep. Here the difficulty is length: five or six weeks of walking, with hills that never quite stop, and weather that can wear you down more than the climbs do.

The road does not feel the same from one region to the next. The Basque Government says the first stretch, in Gipuzkoa, was far from a comfortable walk, because the Oiartzun, Urumea, Oria, Urola and Deba rivers each break the coast, and the path must climb out of one valley and into the next. Spain's national tourism site calls the road through inland Bizkaia one of the most rugged and hardest on the whole Camino, with mountain paths. Of Cantabria it says the opposite: easy walking, with plenty of road and track. The Xunta de Galicia rates its part of the route medium. Its first Galician stage, out of Ribadeo, is the only one it rates high.
What to expect underfoot

The Confraternity of St James says the road has more walking on tarmac than the Camino Francés, with some good sections that make the journey worthwhile. Because it runs parallel to the sea it crosses many rivers, and it says you will often not be in sight of the sea for many kilometres. Waymarking is very good in Galicia and the Basque Country, it says, but occasionally confusing in Cantabria and Asturias.

Pilgrim lodging is enough, it adds, but not as plentiful as on the Camino Francés, and quite a few places open only in summer. That makes the weeks at either end of the season harder to plan, and it is one more reason to read "When to go".
Who it suits

It suits someone with five or six weeks to spare, or someone who will walk it in parts: it divides naturally by region, and each of the four chapters of days in this book is a real walk of one to two weeks. It suits someone who likes the sea beside the path and a different town every evening, and who does not mind that the sea is sometimes hidden behind a motorway. It suits those who can walk in the rain, because on this coast you should expect some.

It is a good second Camino for someone who has walked the Francés and wants something quieter, and, by the Confraternity's account, a possible first one for someone who wants something longer. Beginners can walk it. They should start gently, and for the first days they should expect the Basque hills.
Who should choose another
If you have two weeks or less, a shorter Camino fits better.
The English Way
in this series covers a walk of six days, and
To the End of the Earth
covers the road from Santiago to the sea.
If you want the great social road, with the largest number of pilgrims and the most lodging, the Camino Francés is that road.
The French Way
in this series covers it.
If you want a short, steep and demanding walk, look at the Camino Primitivo.
The Original Way
covers it, and the chapter on other roads in this book explains how the Norte and the Primitivo are joined.
If you dislike road walking, or the thought of a boat crossing worries you, read the days of the first three regions before you decide. Parts of the coast are tarmac.
A word on honesty

This book was written from public sources and not from a walk. It can tell you what the official pages say about a day. It cannot tell you how a day felt. For that, ask people who have walked it, and use the CaminoPlus app for the live answer on beds, boats and weather.
The short answer

The Confraternity of St James says that, for the weather, any time from May to early October is best. The weather on the northern coast, it says, can be very changeable, from fine summer days to very damp and cold autumn ones, and along the coast the very hot, dry conditions found further south are unusual. The rest of this chapter says what that means.
Rain and temperature
This is the green side of Spain, and the green comes from rain. These figures come from Wikipedia's climate tables, which use national weather data. Treat them as patterns, not forecasts.

items.t: San Sebastián

(the weather station at its airport, at Hondarribia, 1991 to 2020): about 1,750 mm of rain a year, on about 143 days with at least a millimetre, which is more than one day in three. November is the wettest month. The average day is about 9 °C in January and about 22 °C in August.
Santander
: drier, about 1,070 mm a year on about 128 rainy days. The average day is about 11 °C in January and about 21 °C in August. November is the wettest month here too.
Santiago

: the table gives about 1,530 mm a year, while the article's text says about 1,800 mm. Either way it rains, and the wettest months fall in autumn and early winter. The average day is about 9 °C in January and about 20 °C in August.

spans.t: Heat is rarer on this coast but not impossible. The record for Santander's downtown station is about 40 °C, in August 1940. Carry water and sun cream in summer.
Daylight

A standard solar calculation gives about nine hours of daylight at the December solstice and about 15.4 hours at the June solstice, for Irun, Santander and Santiago alike. On 1 October there are about 11.6 hours, and on 1 November about 10. From late autumn to early spring, plan to finish each day early.
Crowds and beds

The northern coast is a holiday coast, and its summer is short. The Confraternity warns that in the height of the summer season lodging can be scarce near the most popular places, and that you should be ready to adapt. It suggests that local buses or trains may take you to a bed a few kilometres from the busiest resorts. The Basque Government's brochure says the same from the other side: many pilgrim hostels open only in summer, and you should plan the next day's stage. Walking towards the start or the end of the year, find out what is open before you leave.
Two Basque festivals fall at the start of the road. The Basque brochure says that on 30 June Irun holds its
alarde
, a parade that descends from the old annual muster of arms, and that Hondarribia holds its own on 8 September.
2027 is a Holy Year

A Jacobean Holy Year falls when 25 July, the feast of St James, is a Sunday. That happens in 2027 and again in 2032. In a Holy Year the Holy Door of the cathedral is opened, and Wikipedia says the botafumeiro is used at all the Pilgrims' Masses. Santiago may be busier in such a year, so do not plan a tight connection on the day you arrive.
A season at a time

items.t: Spring (March to May).
Daylight grows from about 11 hours on 1 March to about 12.7 on 1 April. The Confraternity's good weather starts in May. Before that, rain is likely and some hostels have not yet opened.
Summer (June to August).
The warmest months, and the busiest on the coast. Lodging is tightest near the popular places, so find out before you go.
Autumn (September to November).
The Confraternity's good weather lasts into early October. After that the rain returns, San Sebastián's wettest month is November, and the days are down to about ten hours.
Winter (December to February).
About nine hours of daylight, a lot of rain, and many hostels closed for the season. Plan every night ahead.

spans.t: Check before you go
: closures, boat times and the weather change from year to year.
Your credencial

The credencial is the pilgrim's passport, and the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says how to get one. There is an official model, a card of sixteen concertina-folded pages. You can request it in person at the Office, or from institutions the cathedral has authorised, such as parish churches, associations of friends of the Way, pilgrim hostels and confraternities. In Spain and abroad some associations are authorised to issue their own, and there is also a digital credencial, as an app. Stamps are collected mostly where pilgrims sleep, the Office says, but also in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, town halls and other places.

At the start of the road, the Basque Government's brochure says the simplest way to get a credencial is at Irun's pilgrim hostel or at a church in the town. Hours change, so check. Get it before your first night, and have it stamped every day.
Getting to Irun, and home from Santiago

Irun sits on the border, across the Bidasoa from Hendaye in France. Wikipedia notes that its railway station is a major break-of-gauge point, where the French and Spanish railways meet, so a journey from France may mean changing trains at the border. The airport named for San Sebastián stands at Hondarribia, which is Irun's neighbour on the estuary, and the Basque brochure starts its first day from either town. From Hendaye you can walk across the Santiago bridge and begin.
At the other end, the last day passes Lavacolla, near Santiago's airport, as the Xunta de Galicia notes. Timetables change, so plan the way home with them in front of you, not at the last minute.
Training

Walk, with the pack you will carry, and on hills if you can find them. The Asturias tourism pages advise starting a few months before, with comfortable shoes you have worn before. Test your shoes on at least one long day, in the rain. Start at an easy pace and keep it: this road is long.
What to carry

Official advice differs on weight. The Asturias pages say the pack should not pass ten kilos. The national tourism site says seven kilos and not more than a tenth of your body weight. Aim for the lower figure. Both lists agree on the essentials: sun cream, a waterproof jacket, a basic first-aid kit, a torch (a head torch is useful) and light sandals for the evening. The Asturias pages also call a walking stick indispensable. On a coast with this much rain, add a waterproof cover for the pack, and a dry bag for one dry set of clothes.

The Basque Government's brochure adds advice for the whole road: carry your identity document, your credencial and some money or a card, and take care with valuables. Carry enough food and water for each day and a first-aid kit. Choose shoes and clothes for the forecast, and keep your phone's battery charged. Save your maps before you set out, with the CaminoPlus app or any other, because signal is not guaranteed.
Shoes and feet

The national tourism site suggests waterproof hiking boots, half a size larger than usual, already worn in. On a wet road, shoes that dry fast and a spare pair of socks matter a great deal. Treat a hot spot at once, before it becomes a blister.
Waymarks

Follow the yellow arrows and the scallop shells. The Confraternity says the road is very well marked in Galicia and the Basque Country, and sometimes confusing in Cantabria and Asturias. On some coastal sections the yellow arrows share the way with the red-and-white bars of a long-distance footpath (a GR route), and on some routes arrows marked "bici" are for cyclists. The Basque brochure gives one rule that holds everywhere: follow the official marks, and if you meet yellow arrows that point to a different line, do not follow them.
Three boats

The Confraternity says there are typically three places on this road where you take a boat: at Pasaia (Pasajes), across the bay from Laredo to Santoña, and from Somo to Santander. At Pasaia the official route itself uses the boat. At the other two, Cantabria's official definition treats the boat as an option and describes the way round on foot. Boats run to their own timetables and seasons, and the weather can stop them.
Check before you go
, and have a plan for the day the boat does not run.
Language

Spanish is understood everywhere. In the Basque Country you will see signs in Basque as well, and names such as Donostia for San Sebastián. In Asturias, official pages give place names in both Spanish and Asturian, and in Galicia the Xunta uses Galician. A few words of Spanish make every evening easier.
Money and phone
Carry some cash and a card, as the Basque brochure advises. Beyond that, this book gives no prices: they change, and the app and the people at the door are the right source.

chapters.title: The Basque Country: Irun to Kobaron

spans.t: The character of these days

Eight days of hills, sea and old industry. The first three run along the Gipuzkoan coast, where the road climbs out of one river valley and drops into the next. Then it turns inland through the valleys of Bizkaia to Gernika and Bilbao, and ends along the old mining shore of the ría, at the last village before Cantabria.

The distances come from the Basque Government's tourism portal, whose eight stages add up to ~181 km. For the first day the Basque Government's brochure gives a slightly different figure, and the book says so. Official Basque pages give names in Basque and Spanish; this book uses the Spanish form and gives the Basque one where it differs. Many pilgrims split these days differently. This book follows the official stage towns.
Day 1: Irun to San Sebastián (~24 km)

The road starts with a climb. From the Santiago bridge a cycle path follows the estuary into Irun. Just past the town hall the Coast Way and the Interior Way part, and you keep right. The road passes through Hondarribia's old town and climbs to the sanctuary and fort of Guadalupe, with views over the bay of Txingudi. The official way over Jaizkibel begins with a steep ascent and follows the ridge past towers from the second Carlist war; some pilgrims take a track round the mountain's side instead. Then comes the descent to Lezo and Pasai Donibane, and the first boat of the road, across the bay to Pasai San Pedro. The Basque brochure gives ~24.6 km, the portal ~23.8 km from Hondarribia.
Check the boat before you set out.
Day 2: San Sebastián to Zarautz (~23 km)

The road leaves the city past the Miramar palace and the Antiguo district and goes round the slopes of Igeldo, where the Basque heritage list for the stage names a megalithic site. It reaches the Oria at Orio, a small old town with the hermitage of San Martín. The portal says an interpretation centre for the Way, covering both the coast and the interior roads, stands in Orio, close to Zarautz. The day ends in Zarautz, with its old town and the Narros palace. It is a little shorter than the first day, and it still goes up and down.
Day 3: Zarautz to Deba (~21 km)

Two ports and a climb. The road passes the hermitage and causeway of Santa Bárbara and reaches Getaria, whose old town and Monte San Antón are on the Basque list. Then comes Zumaia, with its hermitage of Santiago and its old streets, and the climb to Itziar, where the national tourism site points to the black Virgin, one of the most venerated statues of the area. From there the road drops to Deba. The same site singles out Zarautz and the ports of Getaria and Zumaia for their sea views.
Day 4: Deba to Markina-Xemein (~22 km)

The road leaves the sea here. The Basque list for the stage names the old town of Deba and the Sasiola convent, the old town and port of Mutriku with the hamlet of Astigarribia, and the tower and ironworks of Antsotegi. The Basque Government says the landscape changes as you enter Bizkaia at Markina-Xemein: the broken Gipuzkoan coast gives way to the calm valleys of Lea-Artibai. Carry food and water for the day.
Day 5: Markina-Xemein to Gernika (~25 km)

A day of valleys and small villages. The Basque list names Markina's fronton, the "university of pelota", the collegiate church of Cenarruza at Bolibar, and the towers and country churches of Mendata and Arratzu. The national tourism site calls the road through inland Bizkaia one of the most rugged and hardest on the Camino, with mountain paths and quiet forests. You arrive in Gernika-Lumo, home of the Casa de Juntas, the assembly house of Bizkaia. The portal gives ~24.8 km.
Day 6: Gernika to Bilbao (~30 km)

The longest day in the Basque list. The road leaves Gernika by the Roman site of Forua and goes by Muxika, Larrabetzu, Lezama and Zamudio, where the list names towers, churches and an old town. The list ends with the dolmens of Irumugarrieta, the trenches and fort of Monte Avril, and the sanctuary of Begoña, above Bilbao. The portal gives ~29.7 km. If you want to cut the day, decide where before you leave Gernika, and ask the app. Bilbao is a big city, and a rest day here is a good use of a day.
Day 7: Bilbao to Portugalete (~20 km)

A short official stage, along the left bank of the ría. You leave Bilbao's old town and pass Barakaldo and Sestao, where the heritage list turns industrial: an old furnace, an ore-loading bay. The day ends in Portugalete, with its old town and the convent of Santa Clara. The Vizcaya transporter bridge joins Portugalete to Getxo, and the national tourism site lists it as a World Heritage site. The portal gives ~19.6 km.
Day 8: Portugalete to Kobaron (~17 km)

A day through the old mining shore. The Basque list for the stage names the miners' village at Trapagaran, an open mining pit at Abanto-Zierbena, and at Muskiz the towers, an old ironworks and the hermitage of Nuestra Señora del Socorro. The day ends at the mining complex of Pobeña and Kobaron, also written Covarón. This is where the Basque Country ends. The Basque Government says the way then opens towards Cantabria by Ontón. The portal gives ~16.8 km.
The character of these days

Eight days of small bays, estuaries and old fishing towns, with two boats on offer and a few very long days. A Cantabrian walking guide to this stretch gives nine stages. This book merges the second and third, and it follows the rest. The national tourism site calls the Cantabrian road easy walking, with plenty of road and track.

The lengths come from that guide, "Caminando por el Patrimonio" (2018), which the Camino Lebaniego website hosts. Its figures are long. The guide does not say what they count, but its nine stages add up to ~225 km, and it says ~250 km for the road through Cantabria, while the national tourism site counts only ~170 km, in seven or eight stages. The official route has detours, to Santoña and round the bay of Santander, that a boat or a shorter way can cut, so a real day may be shorter than its figure. The route description comes from Cantabria's 2015 definition of the Way, published in the official state gazette.
Day 9: Kobaron to Castro Urdiales (~21 km)

The Cantabrian route officially begins at El Haya and passes Ontón. The guide counts ~21 km from El Haya to Castro Urdiales, so add a little for the walk from Kobaron. You climb a mountain road for more than ~6 km, drop into the valley of Otañes and follow an old railway line for ~3 km to Santullán. The way then goes by Sámano into Castro Urdiales. It is the first of the "Cuatro Villas de la Costa", the four medieval coastal towns of the Hermandad de la Marina de Castilla, and it has a Gothic church of Santa María, a castle and a hermitage perched on a crag.
Day 10: Castro Urdiales to Laredo (~35 km)

A very long day. The guide breaks it in two, at El Pontarrón in Guriezo, ~12.9 km from Castro Urdiales, with ~22.5 km to Laredo. The road goes on minor roads by Allendelagua, Cerdigo and Islares, where the official text records the ruins of a pilgrims' hospital. After El Pontarrón it crosses Liendo and the ridge tracks of the Sierra de la Vida, then drops into Laredo, the second of the four towns. Its church of Santa María de la Asunción has a fifteenth-century carving of St James as a pilgrim. Decide in advance where you will break this day.
Day 11: Laredo to Güemes (~35 km)

Another long day, with the second boat. From Laredo's seafront a boat crosses the bay to Santoña. The alternative is on foot by Colindres, over the bridge at Treto that replaced the barge that once crossed the Asón, and by Escalante. Either way, Santoña is part of the route: it was where pilgrims landed after embarking at Laredo, the official text says, as documents of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries record. Everyone then walks back to Argoños. Beyond, a coastal and an inland branch lead to Bareyo, with its twelfth-century Romanesque church of Santa María. From there an inland road runs to Güemes, and a coastal one by Ajo to Galizano.
Day 12: Güemes to Santander (~40 km)

The guide gives ~40 km for this stage. The official text offers a boat from Somo to Santander as an option, and it describes the way round the bay on foot by Pedreña, the shore path, El Astillero and the streets of Maliaño or Guarnizo. The boat shortens the day, but check its times. Santander's cathedral grew from a collegiate church that had a chapel of St James in the fourteenth century, and the official text records several pilgrims' hospitals.
Day 13: Santander to Santillana del Mar (~40 km)

The longest day in Cantabria, much of it on minor roads and tracks beside the motorway and the railway: Santa Cruz de Bezana, Boo de Piélagos, the river Pas (crossed in the Middle Ages by the "Barco de Mogro", a ferry), Mar, Requejada and Barreda. The official text names these places, and this book does not say where to stop, so ask the app. Santillana del Mar has its Romanesque collegiate church with its historiated cloister capitals. The national tourism site notes that access to the original Altamira cave, at Santillana del Mar, is heavily restricted, and that a replica can be visited at the Altamira museum.
Day 14: Santillana del Mar to Comillas (~25 km)

The road goes by Oreña and Cigüenza to Cóbreces, where the abbey of Santa María de Viacoeli stands, and down to the beach of Luaña. Then come Ruiloba and Concha. Comillas is known for its monumental nineteenth- and twentieth-century architecture, including the palace of the Marqués de Comillas and Gaudí's Capricho, as the official text says. It also had a pilgrims' hospital before the sixteenth century, founded with a papal bull.
Day 15: Comillas to San Vicente de la Barquera (~12 km)

A short day. You cross the ría de la Rabia, pass the beach of Oyambre, and reach the Puente de la Maza, successor to a late medieval bridge, over the ría of San Vicente. On the far bank are the ruins of a Franciscan convent of the fifteenth century, and then the medieval town, with its rock castle and its church of Santa María de los Ángeles, which keeps a carving of St James the pilgrim. San Vicente is also where the Camino Lebaniego begins, to the monastery of Santo Toribio.
Day 16: San Vicente de la Barquera to Unquera (~16 km)

The road goes by La Acebosa and the tower of Estrada to Serdio, where a pilgrims' hospital once stood. At Muñorrodero the Lebaniego way forks away. Your road crosses the ría of Tina Menor by a bridge to Pesués, where there was a hospital beside the hermitage of Santiago. A path beside the railway leads to Unquera, and then you cross the river Deva into Asturias.
The character of these days

Eleven days between the sea and the mountains. The Principado de Asturias says the road enters by the ría of Tina Mayor and leaves by the ría of the Eo, with more than ~280 km across twenty-one councils. In the east the mountains come close to the water. In the middle lies a heavily industrialised Asturias, between Gijón and Avilés. In the west wide coastal terraces open out, with blue mountain ranges on the horizon.

The distances come from the official Asturias list, which has thirteen stages from Bustio, in the council of Ribadedeva, to the Eo. Asturias says the list can be stretched or shortened as you like, because there are enough hostels and places to stay. Some of its stages end in hamlets, such as Priesca, Casquita, Villamouros and Outur, so this book names each day by its stage towns and the town it passes. The last two Asturian stages, which turn inland to Vegadeo, appear in the chapter on other roads. Official Asturias pages give Spanish and Asturian names; this book uses the Spanish ones.
Day 17: Unquera (Bustio) to Llanes (~25 km)
The Asturian list begins at Bustio, across the Deva. The road passes Colombres, rich in the houses of the
indianos
, emigrants who made their fortune abroad and came home to build. Then come Buelna and Pendueles, the
bufones

of Arenillas (vertical blowholes that spout sprayed sea on high-tide days), Purón and Andrín. Llanes has its basilica of Santa María, a medieval tower, and the "Cubos de la Memoria" painted by Agustín Ibarrola. Keep well back from cliff edges when the sea is rough. The list gives ~24.7 km.
Day 18: Llanes to Ribadesella (~30 km)

The road runs through Po, Celoriu, Barru and Niembru. Asturias says the view of the church of Nuestra Señora de los Dolores, rising above the marsh between Barru and Niembru, is probably one of the most singular pictures of eastern Asturias. At Naves stands San Antolín de Bedón, one of its best rural Romanesque churches. Then come Villahormes, Piñeres and Cuerres. Ribadesella has the cave of Tito Bustillo, which Asturias calls one of the great Palaeolithic sanctuaries of northern Spain. The list gives ~29.8 km.
Day 19: Ribadesella to Priesca, by Colunga (~29 km)

A long day on the road to the pre-Romanesque church of San Salvador at Priesca. On the way are San Esteban, La Vega, Berbes, Arenal de Morís, La Isla, Colunga and Pernús. Asturias says the building zeal of its early kings reached this country, and that the surprising church at Priesca is their legacy; it also points to the Jurassic Museum near Colunga. The list gives ~28.6 km. If it is too long, break it at Colunga.
Day 20: Priesca to Casquita, by Villaviciosa (~13 km)

A short stage. The road goes by Sebrayu to Villaviciosa, where Asturias singles out the light Romanesque church of Santa María de la Oliva and the house where Charles V spent his first night in the Peninsula. At Amandi, close by, a Romanesque church has an unusual apse. Casquita is a hamlet near Villaviciosa, and it is where the link to Oviedo and the Camino Primitivo leaves the coast. The list gives ~13.0 km.
Day 21: Casquita to Gijón (~26 km)

The road goes by Niévares, the Alto de la Cruz, Pion, El Curviellu and Cabueñes to Gijón. Asturias says the city centre, with its beaches of San Lorenzo and Poniente, the Cimavilla quarter and the hill of Santa Catalina, is like the figurehead of a ship facing the horizon. The list gives ~25.6 km. Gijón is a big city, and a good place for a rest day.
Day 22: Gijón to Avilés (~26 km)

The central industrial strip. Asturias says the silhouette of the Universidad Laboral announces it; the official text calls it the largest building in Spain. The road crosses Monte Areo, where Asturias recommends taking time over a burial-mound necropolis, and goes by El Valle, Tamón and Trasona. Avilés surprises, Asturias says, with its old quarter, with the churches of San Francisco and San Nicolás de Bari, the palace of Camposagrado and Galiana street, and with the modern lines of the Niemeyer Centre. The list gives ~26.2 km.
Day 23: Avilés to Muros de Nalón (~21 km)

The way leaves the industrial area by San Cristoba, La Plata, Piedrasblancas, La Lloba, El Monte and Ranón. Crossing the Nalón at Sotu, Asturias says, marks the entry into the western strip, and you reach Muros de Nalón. The list gives ~21.2 km.
Day 24: Muros de Nalón to Soto de Luiña (~15 km)

A short stage. The way goes by El Pito, where the Selgas estate stands, then Rellayo and the beach of the Concha de Artedo, which Asturias calls beautiful. It ends at Soto de Luiña, with its elegant Baroque church of Santa María. Asturias adds that the road does not pass through Cudillero, but close to it. The list gives ~15.2 km.
Day 25: Soto de Luiña to Villamouros (~20 km)

The road goes by Las Chabolas, Montagudu, Silvascura, Busmarzu and San Playu de Teona. Along this western stretch Asturias points to the quiet of Cabo Busto and to Cadavéu, where the house of Padre Galo still stands, and where, it says, modern Asturian literature began. The list gives ~19.9 km.
Day 26: Villamouros to Outur, by Luarca (~20 km)

The way goes by San Cristuébanu, Queirúas, Caneiru, Caroyas, Barcia and Almuña to Luarca. Asturias calls Luarca one of the most rewarding visits of the stretch, above all for its marine cemetery, with unmatched views over the town and the Cantabrian Sea. Outur lies just beyond. The list gives ~19.7 km.
Day 27: Outur to La Caridad, by Navia (~25 km)

The road goes by Villapedre, Piñera, Villaoril and La Colorada to Navia, where the poet Ramón de Campoamor was born. Then come Jarrio and Cartavio, and La Caridad (A Caridá in Asturian), in the council of El Franco. The list gives ~25.1 km. At La Caridad the road divides, and the chapter on other roads says how.
The character of these days

Ten days in which the sea is left behind. You cross the estuary of the Eo into Galicia at Ribadeo and turn inland through green farmland, small medieval towns and the wide plain of the Terra Chá. You reach the monastery of Sobrado dos Monxes and the Camino Francés at Arzúa, then take the last two days to Santiago.

From Ribadeo the distances come from the Xunta de Galicia, whose pages give ~190 km to Santiago by this road, rate it medium, and divide it into eight stages. The Xunta's one very long stage, from Baamonde to Sobrado, is split here at Miraz, using the Xunta's own sections. The Xunta also describes a second way into Galicia, which the next chapter covers. Galician names follow the Xunta's spelling.
Day 28: La Caridad to Ribadeo (~22 km)

The Asturias list has no stage for this crossing, because it turns inland to Vegadeo. The pilgrim-information sites that publish it give ~21 to ~22 km, so take that as a guide and not a measurement. The road leaves Asturias at the estuary of the Eo. The Spanish Wikipedia says the inland way by Vegadeo was the road for those who did not want to cross the estuary by boat, and that it fell into disuse after the bridge of Los Santos opened in 1987. Ribadeo, the Xunta says, stands on a natural viewpoint above the ría, with a mix of medieval and modern architecture.
Day 29: Ribadeo to Lourenzá (~28 km)

The Xunta rates this stage high, with an estimated duration of 6 hours 45 minutes, the only stage on this road that it rates high. The path follows an old route, perhaps Roman or late Roman, by Ove, Cubelas and Vilela, past the parish of San Pedro de Arante with its fifteenth-century chapel, and through Barreiros, Vilamartín and Gondán. Vilanova de Lourenzá grew round a Benedictine monastery founded in 969 by Count Osorio Gutiérrez, called the Holy Count. The town is known for its
fabas
, beans with a protected geographical indication, and holds a bean festival on the first Sunday of October. The Xunta puts the length at ~28.2 km.
Day 30: Lourenzá to Abadín, by Mondoñedo (~22 km)

A steep climb and a descent on the medieval Camiño da Brea, a name from the Latin for the north wind, the Xunta says, meaning in Galician a strong wind with rain. Mondoñedo is a historic-artistic site and was the provincial capital until 1833; the Xunta mentions its cathedral, its almond cake and its angel's-hair jam. From there the road crosses Mount Pico and Mount Santa Cruz to Abadín. The Xunta gives ~21.9 km, and another way from Mondoñedo, by Lousada and Gontán, is ~17.2 km to Abadín.
Day 31: Abadín to Vilalba (~21 km)

The Xunta says this stage is completely flat. It crosses the Terra Chá, the largest plain in Galicia, with A Limia, where wetlands, stone crosses and washing places mark the way. A medieval bridge over the Arnela and another, with three arches, at Pontevella lead to Martiñán. In 2003 the Terra Chá and the upper Miño were declared a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Vilalba, with its fifteenth-century Andrade tower, is known for San Simón cheese and free-range capons. The Xunta gives ~20.6 km and about five hours.
Day 32: Vilalba to Baamonde (~19 km)

The Xunta says the paths may date from the Middle Ages and the royal roads from the seventeenth century. The road passes Penas Corveiras and crosses the medieval Saa bridge, built of thick slate slabs. It then runs on a strip of land between the A-8 motorway and the Ladra river, where, the Xunta says, you can take a dip in good weather. Baamonde has a fourteenth-century Gothic church of Santiago and a calvary of three stone crosses beside an old chestnut tree with a chapel to the Virgin carved in its trunk. The Xunta gives ~19.0 km.
Day 33: Baamonde to Miraz (~15 km)

The Xunta warns of an especially long stage, ~40 km to Sobrado, rated medium-low at over seven hours. This book splits it at Miraz, using the Xunta's sections of ~7.7 km and ~7.2 km. The road passes the chapel of Santo Alberte, where a popular pilgrimage is held every May, and goes on by Digañe and San Paio de Seixón to Santiago de Miraz. The fortress of San Paio de Narla is a short detour. The Confraternity says the high point of the whole route, ~710 m, comes shortly after Miraz.
Day 34: Miraz to Sobrado dos Monxes (~25 km)

The road runs through small villages, by A Roxica, to O Marco das Pías, where you leave the province of Lugo for A Coruña, and on to Guitizá and its artificial lake. Sobrado, the Xunta says, has a Cistercian monastery of Santa María, founded in 952 as a mixed monastery for men and women, with Renaissance and Baroque parts and a medieval kitchen and chapter house. It was the first in Spain to join the Cistercian order, and it still welcomes pilgrims. The Xunta's sections add up to ~25 km.
Day 35: Sobrado dos Monxes to Arzúa (~22 km)

The Xunta says this day shows Galicia's lush landscape and its country architecture. The road goes by Vilarchao and Carelle, As Corredoiras and Boimorto, and Sendelle, with its twelfth-century Romanesque church. At Arzúa the Norte meets the Camino Francés, and the Primitivo, which joined the Francés at Melide, is on the same road. Arzúa is known for its Arzúa-Ulloa cheese, which has a designation of origin, and its street the Rúa do Camiño recalls the old Camiño de Oviedo. The Xunta gives ~22.2 km.
Day 36: Arzúa to Arca (~18 km)

A gentle day between meadows, oaks and eucalyptus, rated low. The Xunta warns that the road crosses the N-547 several times, and asks you to take special care of the traffic. Hamlets such as A Calzada and Ferreiros have names with Jacobean echoes. The day ends at Arca, also called O Pedrouzo, in the council of O Pino, the last before Santiago. The Xunta gives ~18.4 km.
Day 37: Arca to Santiago (~20 km)

The last day. The road passes Lavacolla, near the airport, where, the Xunta says, pilgrims once washed in the stream, and climbs to Monte do Gozo, ~380 m, where pilgrims first saw the cathedral. By the Xunta's account the first to reach the summit was proclaimed king of the pilgrimage. Then the San Lázaro quarter, the Porta do Camiño and the pedestrian streets lead to the cathedral. The Xunta gives ~20.2 km and about five hours.

chapters.title: Other roads, and other ways to split the days

spans.t: Two ways into Galicia
At La Caridad the road divides. The days of this book take the way to Ribadeo, which the Xunta de Galicia lists first, at ~190 km from Ribadeo to Santiago.

The other way is the one the Asturias list follows. It turns inland by El Franco, Porcía and Brul to Vegadeo (A Veiga), ~25.6 km, then goes on to Abres, ~7.3 km, where it crosses the Eo. The Xunta calls it the road "through Santiago de Abres", ~184 km from there to Santiago. From Abres it runs by Trabada to Mondoñedo, ~31.2 km (~11.6 km to Trabada, ~19.6 km on, a section it rates high), and there it rejoins the main road. Counted to Mondoñedo, that is about 64 km by Vegadeo, against about 59 km by Ribadeo, which includes the unofficial ~22 km of Day 28. The Spanish Wikipedia says the Principado treats this inland way as the official one, and that it fell into disuse after the bridge of Los Santos opened in 1987. Ask locally which way is waymarked.
The Interior Way

At the town hall of Irun the Coast Way and the Camino Vasco del Interior part. The Basque tourism portal describes the Interior Way in seven stages of ~250 km, beginning with ~26.2 km from Irun to Hernani. The Confraternity says it goes through the tunnel of San Adrián, from Hendaye to Santo Domingo de la Calzada on the Camino Francés. It is a different Camino, with its own stages, and it is not covered here. Another branch leaves the coast road at Bilbao: the Basque tourism portal lists a stage of ~34 km to Balmaseda, and the Basque Government says it follows the Kadagua river to meet the Camino Francés in the province of Burgos.
The Lebaniego

At San Vicente de la Barquera the Camino Lebaniego begins, the way to the monastery of Santo Toribio de Liébana, where the relic of the Lignum Crucis, a piece of the Cross, is kept. The Cantabrian walking guide says it shares the coast road as far as Muñorrodero and then forks, and it gives three stages, ~28.5, ~31.3 and ~12.1 km. The Confraternity describes a tributary route onward to Mansilla de las Mulas on the Camino Francés. Sources differ on its length, from ~55 km to ~72 km, so check before you plan it.
The links to the Primitivo
The two roads join the Camino Francés at different places: the Primitivo at Melide, the Norte at Arzúa. Between the coast and Oviedo, where the Primitivo begins, Asturias publishes two links.

The first leaves the coast at Casquita, near Villaviciosa, and climbs inland in two stages, ~21.6 km to La Pola Siero and ~17.1 km on, ~38.7 km in all. After San Pedru de Ambás there are two options, the official way or a detour to the monastery of Valdediós, and they meet again at the Alto de la Campa. The Confraternity says some pilgrims leave the coast at Villaviciosa for Valdediós and continue to Oviedo, where they join the Primitivo.

The second joins Avilés and Oviedo in one stage of ~28.8 km, by Cayés, Solís and Nubledo, through four councils. Asturias says many pilgrims, after visiting the Saviour in Oviedo cathedral, went north to Avilés, then the main Asturian seaport.
The Primitivo then runs ~320 km to Santiago, according to the app's catalog.
The Original Way
in this series covers it.
A shortcut from Baamonde

The Xunta describes a shorter way from Baamonde, ~8 km shorter, straight to Sobrado. It meets the main road again near Boimil and leaves it, without passing Arzúa, by Santiso, and the Xunta says it joins the Camino Francés near Santiago's airport. Ask locally about its waymarks before you take it.
Other ways to split the days
This book follows thirty-seven days, but the official lists differ, and many pilgrims split the road differently:

items.t: In the Basque Country
the Basque tourism portal has eight stages, from Hondarribia to Kobaron.
In Cantabria
the walking guide has nine stages, and the national tourism site recommends seven or eight.
In Asturias
the official list has thirteen stages, which Asturias says can be divided as often as you like.
In Galicia
the Xunta has eight stages from Ribadeo, and this book splits the long one at Miraz.

spans.t: The longest days are in Cantabria (Days 10 to 13, ~35 to ~40 km), then Day 6 in the Basque Country (~30 km) and Day 29 in Galicia (~28 km). Boats and shorter alternatives shorten some of them. Where the beds are changes from season to season, so use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
Albergues, and what to expect
An
albergue

is a pilgrims' hostel: bunks in a shared room, a place to wash clothes, and a stamp for your credencial. The national tourism site explains how they work. Some public hostels ask for a donation to cover cleaning and upkeep, and private ones cost a little more. They cannot be booked, and places go first come, first served, with pilgrims on foot ahead of those on horseback and those on bicycles. They usually open around midday. They ask for silence after nine or ten at night, and you leave in the morning by eight or nine.

The Pilgrim's Office adds the spirit of it. Hostels that receive no subsidy are kept going, in austerity, by the contributions of pilgrims, and groups with a support car are asked to find other lodging. The host of a hostel is a
hospitalero

On this road, the Confraternity of St James says, pilgrim lodging is enough, but not as plentiful as on the Camino Francés, and quite a few places open only in summer. The Basque Government says the same: plan the next day's stage. The Asturias pages say the region has enough lodging to let you stop when your feet tire, and the Confraternity adds that there are many campsites, many of them in Asturias with tents to hire for pilgrims. Which towns have a bed this month belongs to the CaminoPlus app and to a phone call.
Sharing a room

A room of bunks asks for a little good manners. Pack your bag the night before, and leave the room quietly at dawn. Use earplugs and an eye mask, because someone will snore. Keep your pack off the floor and your things in one place, and shake out your sleeping bag in the morning. If you see signs of bedbugs, tell the host at once, and wash and dry everything on a hot cycle before it goes back in your pack.
Eating
The national tourism site says some places offer a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask. Each region has its own dishes, and the official pages name some of them:

items.t: Basque Country.

Pintxos, the small bites eaten at the bar, in Bilbao and San Sebastián, and cider, with a cider-house season that, the Basque brochure says, runs from January to April in places such as Oiartzun, Astigarraga and Hernani.
Cantabria.
The national tourism site names anchovies from Santoña and velvet crab from Noja.
Asturias.
Fabada, a bean stew, the cachopo, and desserts such as
frixuelos
and rice pudding, with local cider.
Galicia.
Lourenzá's beans, Mondoñedo's almond cake, Vilalba's San Simón cheese and Arzúa-Ulloa cheese, and the almond Tarta de Santiago.

spans.t: Drink water often and eat before you are hungry. The Basque Government's brochure asks you to carry food and drink for each stage, which matters on days that pass few villages.
Rest days

Take them. The road is long, so plan rest days into the weeks. The cities are natural places for one: San Sebastián, Bilbao, Santander, Gijón and Avilés, and Asturias says Gijón and Avilés each ask for an unhurried walk through their streets. Santillana del Mar and Mondoñedo are small towns with old centres. Do not turn a rest day into a second walk. Wash, sleep, look at your feet, and eat something local.
Check before you go
: opening seasons, boat times and local festivals change from year to year.
Feet

Most of the trouble on a long walk starts in the feet. Wet feet blister, so change socks at lunch, air your feet whenever you stop, and treat a hot spot the moment you feel it. Shoes should be worn in, and half a size larger than usual, as the national tourism site advises. If a blister or a swollen foot will not settle, rest, and see a doctor or pharmacist before it becomes an infection. Do not walk on through pain that gets worse.
Rain, cold and wet

The Confraternity of St James says the weather can run from fine summer days to very damp and cold autumn ones. Carry a waterproof jacket, which both the national tourism site and the Asturias pages recommend, and one dry layer in a dry bag. Wet stone, wet leaves and wet tarmac are slippery, especially on descents and steps, so shorten your stride and use poles if you carry them. In cold rain, stop before you are chilled and put on the dry layer. When the weather turns, stopping early is a sound decision.
Road and path

The Confraternity says there is more walking on tarmac than on the Camino Francés, and the Xunta de Galicia warns that on the way to Arca the road crosses the N-547 several times, and asks for special care with the traffic. Where you must walk on a road, face the oncoming traffic, keep to the edge, and do not walk it in poor light. The Basque Government gives a rule that keeps you from getting lost: follow the official waymarks, and do not follow yellow arrows that point to a different line.
Sea and cliffs

The path runs close to the sea in places. Asturias describes blowholes that throw sprayed sea into the air on high-tide days. Stay well back from edges and wet rock when the sea is rough, and keep children and dogs close. Some paths cross beaches, and boats do not run in every weather. Have a plan for the day a boat does not run.
Heat and sun

The Confraternity says the very hot, dry conditions found further south are unusual on the coast, but heat is not unknown: the record at Santander's downtown station is about 40 °C. Start early on a hot day, wear a hat, use sun cream, and drink before you are thirsty. The Basque Government asks you to carry food and drink for each stage, and you should carry more on the longer days of Cantabria.
Walking alone, and getting help

The sources differ. The Basque Government's brochure says it is advisable to walk in company, and the national tourism site says it is completely safe to walk alone. Whichever you choose, tell someone your plan and keep your phone charged. Note that signal is not guaranteed everywhere.

The European emergency number is 112. Call it for any real danger, an injury you cannot manage, or a person who has not arrived. Know the name of the nearest village. For anything that worries you, such as chest pain, a fever, a swollen leg or a wound that will not heal, see a doctor. This book gives no medical advice beyond the ordinary: water, rest, an early start, and listening to your body.
When to stop

Stopping is not failing. Stop when the weather is dangerous, when you are ill or injured, when you are too tired to see the path, or when a boat has not run and the alternative is long. A day lost can be made up.

Some people walk this road for faith, and some for sport. Some come after a loss, or before a decision. Some are curious, and some are tired of a screen and a chair. The Way asks none of them for a reason at the door. A path of five or six weeks that follows the sea is long enough for whatever you bring.

The first week is hard on the legs, and for a while the walking is the whole of the day. Later the road runs beside the sea, with long stretches in which the mind is free, and you may find that the thinking you meant to do on the last day starts on the fifth.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, or one a week, or none. Let them walk with you, not ahead of you.

items.t: What did you bring that you do not need? Think of the pack, and then of the rest.
What would you say to the person you were a year ago?
Who are you walking for, and do they know?
What do you notice here that you would hurry past at home?
What would you like to still be doing in a year, and what can you begin today?
Is there something you need to forgive, or to ask forgiveness for?

spans.t: Sea and silence

The sea is the companion of this road. On the days it is with you, it makes a daily rhythm: tide, wind and light. On the days it goes out of sight, as it does on the inland stretches of Bizkaia and Galicia, notice whether you miss it. The Way may be as much about what you leave behind as about where you arrive. You do not have to find that. You only have to walk.
Alone and with others
Some of the best days are walked in silence, and some in company. The hostels and the long evenings make company easy. Allow yourself the silence too. The Way will not mind either.
If you are walking for a faith

The Way is a Christian pilgrimage, and its churches and hospitals were built for pilgrims. Pray, or sit in a church, or light a candle, or only listen. If you walk for another reason, you are welcome too. The chapter on arriving says what the Pilgrim's Office writes about its certificates, in its own words.
The last streets

On the last day you leave Arca for Santiago, past Lavacolla and up to Monte do Gozo, ~380 m, where pilgrims first saw the cathedral. The Xunta de Galicia then describes the way in: a descent of about 5 km through the San Lázaro quarter, the Porta do Camiño, and the pedestrian streets and squares of Casas Reais, Cervantes and Acibechería, to the cathedral. Wikipedia says its construction began in 1075 and that it was consecrated in 1211. It is a Romanesque church with later Gothic and Baroque parts, and the Baroque façade on the Obradoiro square, completed in 1740 by Fernando de Casas Novoa, has behind it the Romanesque Pórtico da Gloria of Master Mateo, dated 1188.

2027 is a Jacobean Holy Year. The Holy Door is opened only in Holy Years, and the Xunta says that in a Holy Year the alternative way into the cathedral is the Holy Door at A Quintana. Pilgrims' Masses are held in the cathedral, and Wikipedia says the botafumeiro, the great censer, is used at all of them in a Holy Year. Their times change, so ask on the day.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Compostela is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.
From Irun the road is ~820 km, far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for.
At the Pilgrim's Office

You will need your stamped credencial. To collect the Compostela you take a ticket with a QR code, which lets you follow your place in the queue, and the Office says that in times of great influx it cannot guarantee same-day collection. Its page says the Office is closed on 25 December and 1 January. Procedures and hours change, so look at the Office's own website before you arrive, and do not plan a tight connection for the same day.
Whatever the Compostela means to you, it is a record of a road you walked, not a measure of it.
The next day
Do not leave on the morning after you arrive. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it rewards a second day.

items.t: Rest.
After thirty-seven days your legs have earned it.
See the cathedral without a queue behind you.
Sit in a square and watch the others arrive.
Think about what comes next.
If you want to keep walking, the Camino to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km, goes on from Santiago, and has its own book in this series,
To the End of the Earth
Plan your way home
with the timetables in front of you, not at the last minute.

spans.t: The first days at home can feel odd. The early alarm may now wake nobody. The pack that held everything you needed sits empty on the floor, and the list of things you thought you needed may be shorter than it was. This is ordinary, and it passes.
Keep what you can

items.t: Walk.
A short walk each day, even in the rain, keeps the rhythm of the road and keeps your legs in shape.
Write it down.
Write what you remember while it is fresh: the people, the places, a smell, a hill. Your credencial, with its stamps, is a record too. Keep it somewhere you will see it.
Keep one small habit.
The morning start, the evening wash of the socks, the silence before breakfast. Choose one to carry into ordinary days.
Tell your story, and listen to others'.
Some people will not understand, and that is fine. Others will have walked.
Say thank you.
To the hosts, to the people who kept your house, to the ones who walked with you.

spans.t: Walking again

Some people want to walk again. The Camino Primitivo, which the Norte can join, and the road to the end of the earth at Finisterre and Muxía each have a book in this series, and the app lists other routes. There is no hurry. A Camino can wait, and so can you.
Buen Camino
, today and the day after.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. The Camino del Norte is on its list of routes, but this book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today, so look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, boats, closures and weather.
A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in any app is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Basque Government
, on its tourism and heritage pages: the stages of the Camino de la Costa in the Basque Country and their lengths, the brochure for the first day, and the heritage list by stage.
Cantabria

: the government agreement of 15 October 2015 that defines the Camino de Santiago de la costa through Cantabria, published in the official state gazette, and the walking guide "Caminando por el Patrimonio", for the stages and their lengths.
The Principado de Asturias tourism pages
(turismoasturias.es), and its official Camino brochure: the Camino de la Costa and its thirteen stages, the two links to the Camino Primitivo, and the practical information for pilgrims.
The Xunta de Galicia
, on its official Camino de Santiago portal: the Northern Way, its stages and sections, and the stages Arzúa to Arca and Arca to Santiago.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
: the pages on the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance.
The Confraternity of St James
: its page on the Camino del Norte.
Spain's national tourism site
(spain.info): the page on the Northern Way.
Wikipedia

, for climate tables, the 2024 share of the route, and history: the articles on the Camino de Santiago, Irun, San Sebastián, Santander, Santiago de Compostela, its cathedral, the Jacobean Holy Year, the UNESCO listing, and the Spanish article on the Camino de Santiago de la Costa.
The Spanish government's news item of 5 July 2015
on the UNESCO listing, for the length it gives the coastal route.
A few pilgrim-information websites
, only for the unofficial ~21 to ~22 km of Day 28, named in the fact ledger.
A standard solar calculation
, for the hours of daylight.
The CaminoPlus route catalog
, for the route's start, end, ~820 km and difficulty rating.

spans.t: Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance in this book is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, the book says nothing, and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages and towns who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Alarde
: a Basque parade that descends from an old muster of arms.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabildo
: the governing council of the cathedral.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Indiano
: an emigrant who made a fortune abroad and came home to build.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Pintxo
: a small Basque bite eaten at the bar.
Ría
: a long sea inlet where a river meets the ocean.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
